<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and the README content, Peer Calls v4 is a full-stack WebRTC application that provides peer-to-peer calling functionality with optional SFU behavior. The project is split between a robust backend—written in Go and structured around various server packages—and a feature-rich frontend built with React/Redux and TypeScript. Here’s how to draw a detailed system design diagram capturing its architecture:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Backend Server: Represent the Go-based server as the core processing unit. Inside this component, illustrate submodules such as:
     - Signaling and WebSocket communication (e.g., “wsadapter.go”, “wsclient.go”, “server/ws”).
     - Call control and room management (e.g., “room.go”, “roommanagerfactory.go”).
     - ICE, media handling, and WebRTC functionalities (use of pion/webrtc and related files under “server/codecs”, “server/transport”, “server/udptransport2”, etc.).
     - SFU functionality support when enabled (look under “server/sfu” and configuration via environment variable NETWORK_TYPE, as well as SFU transport nodes in deploy manifests).
     - Pub/Sub mechanism (files under “server/pubsub”) for distributing events across modules.
     - Other cross-cutting concerns like logging (modules under “server/logger” and “server/logformatter”), configuration reading, and metrics (Prometheus integration with “server/prometheus.go” and “server/pubsub/prometheus.go”).
   
   • Frontend Client: Represent the client application (located under “src/client”) that includes:
     - The React/Redux user interface (components like “App.tsx”, “Chat.tsx”, “Video.tsx”, “Sidebar.tsx”, etc.).
     - Interaction with WebSocket and signaling layer (files in “src/client/ws” and related actions).
     - Media processing and handling of peer streams (audio and video components, codecs, and webworker integration).

   • Configuration & Deployment:
     - Deployment artifacts: Represent Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, Kubernetes manifests (deploy/ and kustomization.yaml) as external deployment and orchestration components.
     - Environment variables and YAML-based configuration for setting runtime behavior (e.g., selecting between mesh and SFU mode, Redis configuration, TLS settings).
     - Redis (when enabled) for distributed state management (as indicated by “PEERCALLS_STORE=redis”), which can be shown as an external datastore service.

2. Define the Relationships and Data Flows:
   • Show the client (frontend) interacting with the backend server through HTTP/WebSocket connections. Use directional arrows from the React client to the server.
   • Within the backend, draw arrow flows from the signaling module to the ICE and media processing modules to depict how WebRTC negotiations (offer/answer, ICE candidate exchange, etc.) are handled.
   • Illustrate the optional SFU component that, when enabled (via NETWORK_TYPE=sfu), routes media streams differently—reducing client bandwidth consumption.
   • If Redis is configured, draw an arrow from the backend’s state management (or pub/sub) component to an external Redis service.
   • Represent log, metrics, and monitoring flows (for example, Prometheus metrics exposed via “/metrics”) as side channels that connect to monitoring/alerting systems.
   • Optionally, include arrows for external TURN and STUN servers (referenced in environment variables and the README) that assist with NAT traversal.

3. Emphasize Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular design: The backend is neatly split into specialized packages (e.g., codecs, transport, logging, room management) that communicate internally.
   • Separation of concerns: Distinct layers for signal processing, media handling, and configuration management.
   • Extensibility and configuration-driven behavior: The use of environment variables and YAML configuration (plus the optional SFU mode and Redis store) should be highlighted.
   • Full-stack separation: Frontend and backend are clearly separated with their own technology stacks, yet they integrate tightly through standardized protocols (HTTP, WebSocket, WebRTC).

4. Relevant Technologies & Frameworks to Annotate:
   • Golang, using libraries such as pion/webrtc and go-chi/chi in the backend.
   • React, Redux, and TypeScript for the client.
   • Docker, Kubernetes (for deployment manifests), and GitHub Actions/CI (as seen in the CI/CD config files).
   • Optional Redis store for scalable multi-instance deployments.
   • Prometheus for monitoring.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For this full-stack WebRTC solution, visually separate the frontend from the backend. Use one color (or shape) for the client (e.g., a blue rectangle labeled “Frontend - React/Redux”) and another color (e.g., a green rectangle for “Backend - Go Server”).
   • Under the backend, break down internal components as submodules:
         - “Signaling & WebSocket Communication”
         - “ICE/Media Processing & WebRTC Negotiation”
         - “SFU Module (if enabled)”
         - “Room & Call Management”
         - “Logging, Configuration, and Monitoring”
         - “Pub/Sub and Data Distribution”
   • Use directional arrows (with clear labels) to indicate data flow between client and server, as well as internal communication between modules within the backend.
   • Include external services/components such as Redis, TURN/STUN servers, and deployment orchestration (Kubernetes) outside your main boundary, with arrows pointing to/from the central server.
   • Consider using icons or shapes (for instance, cylinders for databases/Redis, cloud shapes for external services, rectangles for application modules) to make the diagram intuitive.

6. Drawing the Diagram:
   • Start with a high-level overview that separates client and server.
   • Drill down on the server side into its various packages either using nested boxes or a layered approach.
   • Clearly label each component and show the relationships with annotations (for example, “calls via WebSocket”, “configures via YAML file”, “publishes metrics to Prometheus”).
   • Optionally, you might add a “Deployment” zone where Docker, Kubernetes manifests, and CI/CD pipelines are depicted to show the integration of developers’ workflows with the production system.

By following these detailed steps and emphasizing clear labels, directional arrows for data flow, and a color/shape-coded breakdown of architecture, you will create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the structure and purpose of Peer Calls v4. This diagram will help your team quickly understand the modular design, internal interactions, and deployment scenarios of the project.
</explanation>
